pos: n. (the small Hebridean island off Mull where Columba founded a monastery in 563, from which the Picts and afterwards the northern English were evangelised)
etymology: Gaelic Ì, simply “the island”, latinised as Iona through a misreading of Ioua; also called I Chaluim Chille, Columba's isle.
biblical_def: Iona is a bare island three miles long off the western coast of Mull, and it is one of the two or three places from which the gospel actually entered Britain. Columba landed there in 563 with twelve companions, built a monastery of wattle and turf, and spent thirty-four years sending men out from it: to the Picts of the mainland, up the Great Glen to Brude's fortress, and out among the islands. The house kept the Celtic reckoning of Easter and the Celtic tonsure, ordered itself under an abbot rather than a bishop, and copied manuscripts; the Book of Kells was very likely begun in its scriptorium. In 635 Oswald of Northumbria, who had been in exile among the Scots, asked Iona for a bishop, and Iona sent Aidan to Lindisfarne, so that the conversion of the northern English came not from Canterbury but from this island. The Norsemen sacked it repeatedly from 795 and the community withdrew to Kells. The dictionary records Iona for the plainest of reasons: a dozen men on a rock in the sea were made the means of converting two nations. Scripture had said the islands would wait for the law and then receive it, and here that is simple history rather than metaphor.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an island as a tract of land surrounded by water; a mission as a sending out with a commission; a monastery as a house of religious retirement; light as that which makes objects visible; and law as a rule of action prescribed by authority.
webster_full: ISLAND, n. A tract of land surrounded by water; a body of land of smaller dimensions than a continent, encompassed by the sea or by a lake or river.
MISSION, n. A sending; the act of sending; persons sent; the duty on which one is sent; commission; charge.
MONASTERY, n. A house of religious retirement, or of seclusion from ordinary temporal concerns; a convent; an abbey; a cloister.
LIGHT, n. That ethereal agent or matter which makes objects visible; also, illumination of mind; instruction; knowledge.
LAW, n. A rule, particularly an established or permanent rule, prescribed by the supreme power of a state to its subjects, for regulating their actions.
corruption_summary: Hebridean island from which Columba evangelised the Picts and, through Aidan, the northern English; the Celtic mission base of Britain.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel travels by men who are sent, and that the smallest and least promising station may be the one God uses. Isaiah had foretold the Servant's patient work in exactly these terms, “and the isles shall wait for his law” (Isa 42:4), and in Iona that waiting ended: the islands received the law and then carried it inland.

Iona is now mostly visited, and the live temptation is to make a holy place out of what was only ever a base of operations. Columba's men did not go there to be somewhere; they went there in order to be sent from there, under a commission that reaches further than any island, “I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles” (Act 13:47). A monastery is not a destination but a lamp, and a lamp is for seeing by: “A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14). The promise given to the Servant and fulfilled through such houses was never confined, “I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles” (Isa 49:6), and pilgrimage to the ruins is a poor substitute for obeying it.

pos: n. (the tidal island off the Northumbrian coast, also called Holy Island, where Aidan settled in 635 and Cuthbert was bishop)
etymology: Old English Lindisfarena ee, the island of the travellers from Lindsey; later called Holy Island from its monastery.
biblical_def: Lindisfarne is a tidal island off the Northumbrian coast, cut off by the sea twice a day, and for a century and a half it was the chief church of the north of England. Oswald asked Iona for a bishop and received Aidan in 635; Aidan set his see on the island and went on foot through Bernicia preaching, with the king as his interpreter at first. Finan and Colman followed him, and after the Synod of Whitby had settled the Easter question against the Celtic reckoning, Cuthbert was made bishop in 685 and died on Farne two years later. The Lindisfarne Gospels were written and illuminated in that house about 700, and Eadfrith who made them was its bishop. In 793 the Danes landed, killed and plundered, and Alcuin wrote from the Frankish court in horror; in 875 the community left altogether, carrying Cuthbert's coffin, and after long wandering settled at Durham. The dictionary records Lindisfarne for the pattern of its work, which was a bishop who walked, and for the warning in its end: the house that converted a kingdom was itself burned, and the gospel it carried outlived the buildings that carried it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bishop as an overseer of a diocese; a flock as a company under one shepherd; to feed as to supply with nourishment; a temple as a place dedicated to divine worship; and waste as desolate, ruined, destroyed.
webster_full: BISHOP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent, ruler or director; in the primitive church, an elder or overseer of a particular church.
FLOCK, n. A company or collection of sheep or other small animals; a Christian church or congregation, in reference to the pastoral relation.
FEED, v.t. To give food to; to supply with nourishment; to furnish with any thing of which there is continual consumption or waste.
TEMPLE, n. A public edifice erected in honor of some deity, and set apart for divine worship.
WASTE, a. Destroyed; ruined; desolate; stripped of inhabitants; lying unoccupied and untilled.
corruption_summary: Tidal island off Northumberland where Aidan set his see in 635, Cuthbert was bishop, and the Lindisfarne Gospels were made; sacked by the Danes in 793.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the bishop who feeds rather than the bishop who presides. Paul addressed the Ephesian elders as overseers with a flock to tend, “to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28), and Peter put the same charge in a sentence that describes Aidan's practice exactly: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly” (1Pe 5:2).

The second thing to name is the live temptation to measure the church by its buildings and its books. Lindisfarne had the finest manuscript in Europe and a bishop every Northumbrian knew, and in 793 the heathen came into it and left it a ruin, which is a thing the Psalter already knew how to say: “O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled” (Psa 79:1). Isaiah grieved over the same loss in the same words we would use for the burnt church on the island, “Our holy and our beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, is burned up with fire” (Isa 64:11). The men went to Durham and the preaching went on, which is the answer to the grief.

pos: n. (the monastery on the Tyne founded in 681 by Benedict Biscop, where Bede spent his life and wrote)
etymology: Old English Gyrwe, the fen people, from gyr, mud or marsh; the house was In Gyrwum, among the fen dwellers.
biblical_def: Jarrow was a monastery on the south bank of the Tyne, founded in 681 when King Ecgfrith gave Benedict Biscop land for a second house to stand with Wearmouth. Biscop had been five times to Rome and brought back books, and his successor Ceolfrith enlarged the library until it was the best in England; out of it came three great pandects of the Latin Bible, of which the Codex Amiatinus survives, carried toward Rome by Ceolfrith in 716. Into that library at the age of seven came Bede, who never travelled further than York and Lindisfarne and who spent fifty years reading, teaching and writing: the commentaries, the chronology that fixed the reckoning of years from the Incarnation, and the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, which is the reason anything is known of the conversion of England at all. He was translating the Gospel of John into English when he died in 735, dictating to a boy until the last sentence was taken down. The dictionary records Jarrow for the library and the lifetime: books bought abroad, a man who stayed home, and a method handed on to Alcuin's generation and from them to the Frankish schools.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a library as a collection of books; a book as a volume in which we read; to teach as to instruct; to commit as to give in trust; and to search as to look over carefully in seeking something.
webster_full: LIBRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution or a company.
BOOK, n. A general name of every literary composition which is printed; but appropriately, a printed composition bound; a volume.
TEACH, v.t. To instruct; to inform; to communicate to another the knowledge of that of which he was before ignorant.
COMMIT, v.t. To give in trust; to put into the hands or power of another; to entrust.
SEARCH, v.t. To look over or through, for the purpose of finding something; to examine by inspection.
corruption_summary: Monastery on the Tyne founded in 681, whose library made Bede and whose pandects of the Latin Bible include the Codex Amiatinus.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the succession of teachers, which is the ordinary way the church's learning has always travelled. Paul states it with four links in one sentence: what was heard from him is to be committed “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). Biscop bought the books, Ceolfrith kept them, Bede read them, and the next century taught from Bede.

The live temptation is to think that scholarship and plain exposition are rivals. Jarrow was both at once: the house that produced the most learned man in Europe also produced the first English Gospel, and its work answers to the pattern set at the Water Gate, where they “read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). The Bereans are commended for the same temper of mind that the Jarrow library served, having “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). Solomon names the condition no library can supply: “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9).

pos: n. (the monastery at the mouth of the Wear, founded by Benedict Biscop in 674, the elder of the twin houses with Jarrow)
etymology: Old English Æt Wiramuthan, at the mouth of the Wear, with monk prefixed to distinguish the monastic settlement from the town.
biblical_def: Monkwearmouth, the house at the mouth of the Wear, was founded in 674 when Ecgfrith gave Benedict Biscop seventy hides of land, and it was the elder of the twin monasteries that were always governed as one. Biscop built it of stone in the Roman manner and sent to Gaul for glaziers, so that glass windows returned to England after two centuries; he brought masons, service books, pictures for the walls, and the chief cantor of St Peter's at Rome to teach the house to sing. Bede entered it as a boy of seven under Abbot Benedict before being moved to Jarrow, and he wrote the lives of its abbots. The two houses together held some six hundred monks at their height. Danish raids and the Conquest ruined it, and the Norman priory that followed was a cell of Durham. The dictionary records Monkwearmouth because it shows what a founder is for: Biscop himself wrote no book and is remembered for no sermon, yet every stone, window, song and volume that made Bede possible was fetched by him. The foundation is not the building; but someone has to lay it, and the men who lay foundations are rarely the men whose names the work carries.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a foundation as the basis of an edifice; a corner stone as the stone which unites two walls; to build as to construct and raise; a mind as intention or disposition; and a wall as a work of stone or brick for defence or enclosure.
webster_full: FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that part of a building which lies on the ground; the act of fixing the basis; the basis or ground work of any thing.
CORNER STONE, n. The stone which lies at the corner of two walls, and unites them; the principal stone, and especially the stone which forms the corner of the foundation.
BUILD, v.t. To frame, construct and raise, as an edifice or fabric of almost any kind.
MIND, n. Intention; purpose; design; inclination; will; desire.
WALL, n. A work or structure of stone, brick or other materials, raised to some height, and intended for a defence or security.
corruption_summary: The elder of the twin Northumbrian houses, founded 674 by Benedict Biscop, who fetched the books, glass, masons and song that made Bede's Jarrow possible.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that founders are servants of a foundation they did not lay. Paul will allow no rival to that one basis, “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11), and the household he describes is built on apostolic teaching with “Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20). Biscop's stone and glass were worth fetching only because that foundation was already laid.

The live temptation runs the other way, toward trusting the apparatus. Monkwearmouth had the best masonry, the best choir and the best library in England, and the Psalter has the answer to any confidence placed in such things: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1). What makes a building project succeed under God is a willing people rather than a grand plan, which is exactly how Nehemiah accounts for his wall: “for the people had a mind to work” (Neh 4:6). Biscop's six hundred monks had that mind, and one boy among them wrote the history of the English church.

pos: n. (the headland priory at the mouth of the Tyne, burial place of King Oswin, repeatedly sacked and later a cell of St Albans)
etymology: Old English Æt Tinanmuthe, at the mouth of the Tyne, the river name being British and of uncertain sense.
biblical_def: Tynemouth stands on a headland above the mouth of the Tyne, a site held in turn by a Roman signal station, an early Northumbrian monastery, a Benedictine priory and a castle, because whoever holds it watches the river. The monastery received the body of Oswin of Deira, murdered in 651 at the instigation of his kinsman Oswiu, and his tomb made the house a place of resort. It was burned by the Danes, refounded, burned again, and in 1090 granted by Robert de Mowbray to the abbey of St Albans, which held it against Durham's claims in a quarrel that ran for a century. The priory and the castle shared one gatehouse; the monks lived inside a fortress and the fortress sheltered behind a church, and both were surrendered in 1539. The dictionary records Tynemouth for the shape of its story rather than for any teaching that came out of it. The relics of a murdered king drew more pilgrims than the preaching of the gospel ever drew, which is a standing warning about what men will travel for. The house was three times destroyed and three times rebuilt in stone, while what cannot be destroyed was never in the stone at all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a relic as the remains of the body of a saint; a tomb as a grave or vault for the dead; an altar as a place for sacrifice; a ruin as destruction or overthrow; and solitary as living alone, lonely.
webster_full: RELIC, n. That which remains; the remains of the body of a saint, or something belonging to a saint, kept with a superstitious reverence.
TOMB, n. A grave; a sepulcher; a vault in the earth for the reception of the dead; a house or building for the dead.
ALTAR, n. A mount; a table or elevated place, on which sacrifices were anciently offered to some deity.
RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; defeat; that change of any thing which destroys it, or entirely defeats its use.
SOLITARY, a. Living alone; not having company; retired; remote from society.
corruption_summary: Headland priory at the mouth of the Tyne, holding the tomb of the murdered King Oswin; thrice destroyed, finally a fortified cell of St Albans.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour Scripture actually gives the slain, which is a place at the altar and a hearing, not a shrine and a fee. John sees them there: “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9), and the great catalogue of the faithful ends with wanderers of whom “the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) and no tomb at all.

The live temptation at a place like Tynemouth is the traffic in relics, which draws crowds that preaching does not draw, and which the dictionary names as a corruption and not a devotion. Micah says what comes of a religion kept up for gain in a holy place: “Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field” (Mic 3:12), and the headland has been plowed three times over. Jeremiah's lament is the right tone for the ruin and not despair: “How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!” (Lam 1:1). The gospel that was preached there survived every burning, because it was never in the masonry.

pos: n. (the Durham headland where Heiu founded the first women's monastery in Northumbria, and where Hilda was abbess before Whitby)
etymology: Old English Heortéu, the stag island or headland, with later pool from the harbour; Bede's Heruteu.
biblical_def: Hartlepool is a headland and harbour on the Durham coast, and its place in English church history is that the first monastery of women in Northumbria was planted there. Heiu, whom Bede calls the first woman in that province to take the veil, founded it about 640 under Aidan's direction, and when she left for Tadcaster, Hilda was set over it in 649 and governed it for some years before moving to found Whitby. Bede says she there established a rule of life taught her by learned men, and the discipline she worked out at Hartlepool is what she carried to the greater house, where kings and bishops came for counsel and five bishops were trained. Early Christian grave markers with Anglian names, several of them women's, have been found on the headland. The Danes destroyed the house and it was never rebuilt. The dictionary records Hartlepool as the quiet first station of a notable work: the gift of hospitality and good order, exercised in an obscure place by women whose names are mostly lost, and then carried where it could be seen. Pure religion is described in Scripture by what it does for the helpless, and such houses did it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hospitality as the practice of entertaining strangers; religion as the performance of our duties to God and men; a stranger as a foreigner or guest; to visit as to go to see for comfort; and order as regular disposition and method.
webster_full: HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.
RELIGION, n. Religion, in its most comprehensive sense, includes a belief in the being and perfections of God, and the practice of all moral duties.
STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; a guest; a visitor.
VISIT, v.t. To go or come to see; to attend, as a physician; to go to see in kindness, or for the purpose of comfort or relief.
ORDER, n. Regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things; a regular government or discipline.
corruption_summary: Durham headland holding the first Northumbrian monastery of women, founded by Heiu about 640 and governed by Hilda from 649 before she founded Whitby.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the scriptural test of a religious house, which is not its architecture or its learning but its care of the helpless. James gives the definition and leaves no room to argue: pure religion is “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27). A house on a cold headland that fed and sheltered people met that test before it met any other.

The second thing to name is the temptation to despise a first and obscure station. Hartlepool is remembered only because of what Hilda did afterwards, and it was at Hartlepool that she learned to do it. Christ counts the plain acts and names them as done to himself: “I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35), and the writer to the Hebrews adds the reason for keeping the door open at all, “for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2). The wisdom that grew in the small house was the wisdom that governed the great one: “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9).

pos: n. (the double monastery on the Berwickshire coast ruled by Abbess Æbbe, burned about 686 after Bede's account of its laxity)
etymology: Old English Coludesburh and Coldingaham, the homestead of Colud's people; the headland is still St Abb's Head.
biblical_def: Coldingham stood above the cliffs of the Berwickshire coast, a double house of men and women under Æbbe, sister of Oswald and Oswiu, from about 640. Cuthbert visited it and prayed in the sea by night; Etheldreda of Ely took the veil there. Bede then tells what happened to it, and tells it without softening: while Æbbe lived the house held, but the cells built for prayer and reading were used for feasting, drinking and gossip, the women wove fine clothes instead of keeping the hours, and a visiting Irishman named Adamnan warned them that the place would burn. Æbbe amended things for a time; after her death the old ways returned, and about 686 the monastery burned to the ground. Bede records the fire as a judgment and names the sins that brought it. A Benedictine priory was founded on the site by Edgar of Scotland in 1098 and lasted until the Reformation. The dictionary records Coldingham for Bede's honesty. The chronicler who praised Lindisfarne wrote down the disgrace of Coldingham in the same book, because a history written to flatter the church is of no use to the church.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines discipline as instruction and government; a cell as a small close apartment in a monastery; to try as to prove by a test; a fire as the effect of combustion; and waste as that which is desolate or unoccupied.
webster_full: DISCIPLINE, n. Education; instruction; cultivation and improvement; also, correction; chastisement; punishment intended to correct crimes or errors.
CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison; a small cave or hollow place; the hut of a hermit; a small religious house.
TRY, v.t. To examine; to make experiment on; to prove by a test; to purify or refine, as metals.
FIRE, n. Heat and light emanating visibly from bodies in combustion; the agent of combustion and of refining.
WASTE, n. Destruction; devastation; a desolate or uncultivated country; useless expense.
corruption_summary: Berwickshire double monastery under Abbess Æbbe, burned about 686; Bede recorded its laxity and the fire as judgment in the same book that praises Lindisfarne.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church's own records must tell the truth about the church. Bede wrote Coldingham down, and the reason a candid history matters is that the work of every house is going to be assayed anyway: “the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is” (1Co 3:13). The warning is not rhetoric, for the God who dwells among the lamps is himself the assayer: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Heb 12:29).

The live temptation is the one Adamnan named at the door, which is a religious house using its buildings for its own comfort while the work they were built for goes undone. Haggai puts the question to men who had panelled their own houses and left God's a ruin: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). The remedy offered to a failing church is never flattery but a call to hold out: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10). Æbbe amended the house while she lived, and that much Bede also records.

pos: n. (the monastery founded in 673 by Maelrubha on the remote west coast of Ross, long a sanctuary)
etymology: From Gaelic A' Chomraich, the sanctuary; the English name is from the river Apor Crosan, the mouth of the little crossing.
biblical_def: Applecross lies on the west coast of Ross, facing Skye across the Inner Sound and shut off by hills so steep that until the nineteenth century it was reached chiefly by sea. Maelrubha, who came from Bangor in Ireland and was of the kindred of Niall, founded a monastery there in 673 and worked in it for fifty-one years until his death in 722, evangelising Wester Ross and Skye from it. The Gaelic name of the place is simply the sanctuary, and the ground around the church was held as a girth within which no violence might be done, a privilege respected long after the monastery itself had gone. Carved cross slabs survive on the site. The dictionary records Applecross for the pattern of the Celtic mission at its far edge, which was a man going to the most inaccessible coast he could reach and staying there for half a century. Withdrawal of that kind is not escape; the Lord himself sought solitary places in order to pray and then returned to the crowds, and the men who went to Applecross went in order to work. A sanctuary where no blood might be shed was also a standing sermon in a country that settled most things by the sword.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a sanctuary as a sacred place and a place of refuge; solitary as living alone and retired; to withdraw as to retire or go apart; a wilderness as a tract of waste and uninhabited land; and prayer as the asking of a favor of God.
webster_full: SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple; also, a place of protection; a sacred asylum.
SOLITARY, a. Living alone; not having company; single; retired; remote from society.
WITHDRAW, v.i. To retire; to retreat; to quit a company or place; to go apart.
WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings, whether a forest or a wide barren plain.
PRAYER, n. In worship, a solemn address to the Supreme Being, consisting of adoration, confession, supplication and thanksgiving.
corruption_summary: Remote monastery in Wester Ross founded by Maelrubha in 673, long honoured as a sanctuary; the far western edge of the Celtic mission.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that solitude in Scripture is for prayer and then for work, never for its own sake. The Lord's own practice sets the pattern and the rhythm: “rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35), and Luke records it as a habit and not an episode, “And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed” (Luk 5:16).

The live temptation is to dress up avoidance as devotion, or to sneer at every withdrawal as escape. Both miss what Maelrubha did, which was to go as far as a boat would take him and then preach there for fifty-one years. Christ dismissed the crowd in order to pray and then came back to them: “he went up into a mountain apart to pray: and when the evening was come, he was there alone” (Mat 14:23). The Psalmist fixes prayer as the fixed work of the day in any place, remote or crowded: “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud” (Psa 55:17).

pos: n. (the island in the Firth of Forth holding an Augustinian abbey, called the Iona of the east)
etymology: Gaelic Innis Choluim, Columba's island, from innis, an island, and the saint's name.
biblical_def: Inchcolm is a small island in the Firth of Forth, within sight of both shores, with a hermit's cell of rough stone that is among the oldest surviving church buildings in Scotland. Alexander I, driven onto the island in a storm about 1123 and fed by the hermit there, founded a house of Augustinian canons in thanksgiving; it became an abbey in 1235, and its cloister and octagonal chapter house still stand almost whole, which is rare in Scotland. Its position made it a target: English fleets raided it repeatedly in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, and the canons bought off or fled from a succession of them. The abbey was suppressed at the Reformation and the island was afterwards fortified in three separate wars. The dictionary records Inchcolm because it is the eastern counterpart of Iona, a little land in the sea given over to worship, and because of what such places were for. Scripture repeatedly calls the islands and the seafarers to praise: those who do business in great waters see the works of the LORD, and an abbey on a shipping lane in the Forth stood where they could not help seeing it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an isle as a tract of land surrounded by water; the deep as the sea or ocean; to glorify as to honor and magnify; business as employment and occupation; and a wonder as that which excites surprise.
webster_full: ISLE, n. A tract of land surrounded by water, or a detached portion of land embosomed in the ocean, in a lake or river.
DEEP, n. The sea; the abyss of waters; the ocean; any abyss or unfathomable gulf.
GLORIFY, v.t. To praise; to magnify and honor in worship; to ascribe honor to, in thought or words.
BUSINESS, n. Employment; that which occupies the time and attention; affair; concern; mercantile transactions.
WONDER, n. That emotion which is excited by novelty, or the presentation of some object which is unusual; a strange thing; a prodigy.
corruption_summary: Island abbey in the Firth of Forth, founded by Alexander I about 1123 and called the Iona of the east; its cloister survives nearly intact.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the summons of Scripture to the islands and the sea to worship, which is given as a command and not a sentiment. Isaiah calls across the water, “glorify ye the LORD in the fires, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea” (Isa 24:15), and the Psalter makes the isles the very place where the news of God's reign is to be received: “let the multitude of isles be glad thereof” (Psa 97:1).

The live temptation with a surviving cloister is antiquarianism, a love of the stones that outlives any interest in what was done among them. The men on the Forth were set where sailors passed, and the Psalter says exactly what sailors are for: “They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters” (Psa 107:23) are the men who “see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep” (Psa 107:24). An abbey on a shipping lane was a witness to men who were already being preached to by the weather.

pos: n. (the Fife burgh on the Forth, site of a Cistercian abbey of 1217 and of the legends of Serf and Kentigern)
etymology: Gaelic cuileann ros, the holly point, or cul ros, the back of the promontory; the Scots pronunciation keeps the older form.
biblical_def: Culross is a small burgh on the north shore of the Forth in Fife, remarkable for having survived almost unaltered from the seventeenth century. Its church history runs back much further in legend than in record: Serf is said to have had a cell there, and the medieval lives make it the birthplace of Kentigern, whose mother Thenew was supposedly cast adrift and came ashore at Culross to be taken in by Serf. Nothing of this can be verified, and the earliest firm fact is the Cistercian abbey founded in 1217 by Malcolm, Earl of Fife, whose choir became the parish church at the Reformation and still serves. In the seventeenth century the burgh prospered on coal and salt, and Robert Pont and later ministers preached in the abbey church. The dictionary records Culross for the lesson of its sources. A place can be rich in sacred story and poor in sacred fact, and the church has no business receiving a tale merely because it is old and local and flattering. The command is to test, and the standard of testing is the written word, which outlasts every legend told about it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a legend as a chronicle of the lives of saints, often fabulous; a tradition as the delivery of opinions by oral communication; to try as to prove by a test; a witness as one who gives testimony; and the word as that which is spoken or written.
webster_full: LEGEND, n. A chronicle or register of the lives of saints, formerly read at matins; any memorial or relation; an idle or ridiculous story told respecting saints.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; oral delivery.
TRY, v.t. To examine; to prove by a test; to experience; to put to the proof.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; that which furnishes evidence or proof.
WORD, n. An articulate or vocal sound, or a combination of sounds, used by common consent as the sign of an idea; also, the Scriptures.
corruption_summary: Fife burgh with a Cistercian abbey of 1217, whose older fame rests on unverifiable legends of Serf and the birth of Kentigern.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of testing, which Scripture lays on ordinary believers and not only on scholars. John gives the command and the reason in one breath: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world” (1Jo 4:1). A local saint's tale is not exempt from that examination because it is charming or because it is old.

The live temptation is the opposite pair of errors, credulity about pious stories and contempt for the church's past as such. The measure in both directions is the gospel already delivered, and Paul fences it absolutely: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8). What lasts at Culross is not the legend but the text read in the abbey choir, for “the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8), and the faith it carries was “once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) and needs no supplement from the lives of local saints.
